article_title: Language Proficiency and Academic Achievement. Multilingual Matters 10.
citation: Rivera, Charlene, Ed. (1984). Language Proficiency and Academic Achievement. Multilingual Matters 10. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED240882
title: Do not exit students from bilingual programs on face-to-face conversational fluency alone
description: The volume argues that apparent conversational fluency in English is a linguistic facade that can hide large gaps in academically related aspects of proficiency, so exit decisions based on teacher judgements or tests assessing face-to-face skills are likely to set students up for academic difficulty. Because academic proficiency takes considerably longer to develop than surface fluency, exit criteria must rest on a theoretical framework relating language proficiency to academic achievement rather than on intuitive judgements of fluency.
requirements: A theoretical framework relating language proficiency to academic achievement to ground entry/exit criteria
constraints: Relevant empirical studies on threshold levels for effective participation in all-English classrooms remain to be done, per the article
target_learners: Language minority students in bilingual education programs
target_learning_goals: Accurate assessment of academic language proficiency for program exit decisions
examples: The article documents students frequently exited from bilingual classrooms on the assumption that fluent face-to-face English means they can survive an all-English classroom
key_sources: Rivera, Charlene, Ed. (1984). Language Proficiency and Academic Achievement. Multilingual Matters 10. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED240882

article_title: 2023 Pace of Learning Report
citation: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/
title: Dosage-based add-on interventions yield only a student's prevailing pace of learning, so students needing the most help gain the least
description: The brief argues that interventions adding instructional time at the margin — longer days, extra school days, tutoring — cannot retire learning losses because "during the additional period of instruction, a student’s prevailing POL is the best we can expect to realize." It advises treating the pre-COVID POL as an upper bound on gains from added time, since "the students who need the extra help the most are likely to gain the least from the broad application of added learning time."
requirements: Any added-time intervention must be evaluated against the student's historical pace of learning rather than assumed full yield
constraints: The brief lists further drawbacks: interventions are time-limited and funding-constrained, supply challenges exist in needy communities, long-term persistence of short-term impacts is unknown, and voluntary programs may disproportionately serve those who least need them
target_learners: K-12 students with COVID learning losses, especially those with below-average pace of learning
target_learning_goals: Recovering pandemic learning losses toward grade-level benchmarks
examples: A 6th-grade student with a POL of 50 percent and 90 days of loss would reach only 9th-grade level after twelve years, and full tutoring benefit over two years would advance him only a half year
key_sources: Margaret “Macke” Raymond, Ph.D. (2022). The Pace of Recovery after COVID. Center for Research on Education Outcomes, Hoover Institution. https://www.eduref.org/

article_title: The learning curve: Revisiting the assumption of linear growth across the school year
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). The learning curve: Revisiting the assumption of linear growth across the school year. NWEA Research working paper. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19345747.2020.1839990
title: Do not assume linear within-year growth when estimating learning from achievement data
description: Analyses that estimate how much students learn during the school year — for school-year-length policy, summer-loss studies, or gap research — should test rather than assume that within-year growth is linear. The article's own finding is that "assuming linear within-year growth is often not justified, particularly in reading," so linear-growth assumptions can distort such estimates, especially in reading.
requirements: Achievement data at multiple within-year time points (e.g., fall, winter, spring) to check growth shape before fitting linear models
constraints: The evidence reported covers math and reading in grades K-8 in 2016-17; the abstract notes the problem is particularly pronounced in reading
target_learners: Kindergarten through 8th grade students
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement and modeling of within-year academic growth
examples: The authors examined fall, winter, and spring scores for over seven million K-8 students and found the linear assumption often unjustified
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). The learning curve: Revisiting the assumption of linear growth across the school year. NWEA Research working paper. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19345747.2020.1839990

article_title: Practitioner beliefs and behaviors in AI-enhanced education: DOT framework survey evidence
citation: Gibson, D., Azukas, M. E., & Knezek, G. (2025). Practitioner Beliefs and Behaviors in AI-Enhanced Education: DOT Framework Survey Evidence. https://doi.org/10.70725/846858waolmj
title: The DOT Framework: combining Design Thinking and Open Systems theory to guide intentional, human-centered AI-enhanced teaching
description: The DOT Framework combines the iterative logic of Design Thinking (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test) with the Open Systems Model (environment, input, process, structure, output, feedback) to guide Transformation of teaching through intentional AI enhancement. It positions AI as "a co-intelligent collaborator, an adaptive, semi-autonomous cognitive partner whose contributions are shaped and evaluated through ongoing human guidance." The framework operates at micro-system (classroom) and macro-system (institution) levels simultaneously, situating AI use within a pedagogical and institutional ecosystem that values human judgment, iterative refinement, and systemic coherence. The survey provides preliminary descriptive support for it as a model of practitioner beliefs and practices.
requirements: Professional development, policy infrastructure, and institutional feedback loops are positioned as prerequisites for sustainable AI integration at the macro-system level
constraints: The article states current empirical support is preliminary and descriptive rather than confirmatory validation, and the framework's link to instructional outcomes remains untested
target_learners: higher education practitioners
instructors and instructional designers integrating AI
target_learning_goals: purposeful, human-centered AI use in teaching and learning
design-oriented AI integration practices
examples: The survey mapped items conceptually to the framework's design thinking stages and open systems components, and found practitioners strong at Ideate/Prototype but weak at Empathize and Test/Feedback stages
key_sources: Gibson, D., Azukas, M. E., & Knezek, G. (2025). Practitioner Beliefs and Behaviors in AI-Enhanced Education: DOT Framework Survey Evidence. https://doi.org/10.70725/846858waolmj

article_title: Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education
citation: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef
title: Domain-specific GenAI declaration framework translating an activity taxonomy into task-specific disclosure instruments
description: The framework is a design artefact that translates the Bouvier et al. taxonomy of GenAI-mediated activities (Generate, Interpret, Evaluate, Get Feedback, Refine, Brainstorm, Design, Simulate, Reflect) into assessment-facing declaration categories for Computer Science coursework. It comprises two parallel task-specific structures (writing and coding) in which students indicate whether GenAI was used, its extent (Minor, Moderate, Extensive), and provide explanations with example prompts. The authors position it as operating "at the level of thestudent's declaration", complementing policy-level instruments such as the AI Assessment Scale, which operates at the educator's design-decision level.
requirements: Requires accurate self-reporting by students, accompanied by clear institutional guidance on which tools count as GenAI use
constraints: It does not itself detect misconduct
Transferability to disciplines beyond computing remains an open question
The goal is not a precise measurement instrument but a structured way to describe GenAI use
target_learners: Computer Science higher education students, including school-leavers, international students, career-changers, and degree apprentices
target_learning_goals: Academic integrity and transparent disclosure of GenAI use
Student reflection on their own learning process with GenAI
AI literacy and preparation for professional documentation of GenAI workflows
examples: A writing-focused form organised around six activity categories and a coding-focused form with five activity categories, both using the same Minor/Moderate/Extensive extent scale with explanations and example prompts

International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef

article_title: Tool, Tutor, or Crutch?: A Grounded Theory of Cognitive Scaffolding and Offloading in AI-Assisted Programming Education
citation: Liu, D., Fan, G., & Pan, L. (2026). Tool, tutor, or crutch?: A grounded theory of cognitive scaffolding and offloading in AI-assisted programming education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00592-w
title: Domain Mastery versus Tool Mastery tension model with Scaffolding and Offloading loops
description: A grounded-theory process model explaining how learners navigate between Domain Mastery, described as "conceptualization, explanation, and evaluation", and Tool Mastery, "procedural efficiency with AI". The model posits two recurrent feedback loops: a Scaffolding Loop, in which learners inquire, test, modify, and explain AI output while retaining germane processing, and an Offloading Loop, in which rapid delegation suppresses germane processing. It is interpreted through Cognitive Load Theory and Self-Determination Theory and is offered as an interpretive, non-causal account that reconciles the performance–learning paradox.
requirements: Interpretation through Cognitive Load Theory and Self-Determination Theory as primary lenses, with ZPD and Cognitive Apprenticeship as sensitizing concepts
constraints: The article states it describes associations rather than causal mechanisms; loops can co-exist within one assignment and learners move between them over time
target_learners: undergraduate programming students
target_learning_goals: durable conceptual understanding and evaluative skill in programming
examples: Categories emerged from constant comparison across an AI-enabled section and a human pair-programming contrast section over 16 weeks, using interviews, logs, and concept maps
key_sources: Liu, D., Fan, G., & Pan, L. (2026). Tool, tutor, or crutch?: A grounded theory of cognitive scaffolding and offloading in AI-assisted programming education. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-025-00592-w

article_title: LumiNote: LLM-Assisted Multimodal Instruction for VR Stage Lighting Education
citation: Danxuan Liang, Chun Yin Li, Zheng Wei, Xian Xu, Meng Xia, Huamin Qu, Wai Tong. (2026). LumiNote: LLM-Assisted Multimodal Instruction for VR Stage Lighting Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17335
title: Domain-grounded mediation framework for LLM-assisted VR instruction
description: The article frames LLM-assisted VR instruction as a mediation process connecting three layers: expert expression, executable operations, and learner-facing representations. The authors state that their findings characterize LLM-assisted VR instruction as a "domain-grounded mediation process among expert expression, executable operations, and learner-facing representations." In this framework, an instructor's high-level pedagogical intent must be translated into concrete scene manipulations while simultaneously being made understandable to learners. Technical executability alone is insufficient because generated actions must remain inspectable and controllable by the instructor.
requirements: An instructor-facing system that translates pedagogical intent into executable actions within a domain-specific VR environment
Domain knowledge integration into LLM prompting to constrain generation to valid operations
constraints: Focused on instructor-facing live concept delivery rather than dynamic student interaction
Generated actions require instructor review and approval before execution
target_learners: Stage lighting instructors
Beginner-level technical theater arts students
target_learning_goals: Understanding spatial lighting relationships
Connecting technical operations with visual effects
Acquiring domain-specific terminology
key_sources: Danxuan Liang, Chun Yin Li, Zheng Wei, Xian Xu, Meng Xia, Huamin Qu, Wai Tong. (2026). LumiNote: LLM-Assisted Multimodal Instruction for VR Stage Lighting Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17335

article_title: Literacy demands placed on students in student–GenAI entanglements in higher education
citation: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7
title: Dohn's three-level framework of competence demands applied to literacy demands: domain-internal, activity-internal, and activity-framing levels
description: The paper uses Dohn's (2009a, b) context-level framework to analyze literacy demands as context-sensitive expectations placed on students at three interacting levels. The "domain-internal level" concerns domain-specific traits, facts, and perspectives; the "activity-internal level" concerns how the activity is performed, such as integrating GenAI inputs into coherent writing; and the "activity-framing level" concerns how the setting norms the activity, such as institutional expectations about individually authored work. The levels are analytical rather than isolated: demands interact with, frame, concretize, interfere with, and contradict each other, producing a unity of demands negotiated in every concrete situation that may be incoherent.
requirements: The levels are analytical and must be treated as interacting and mutually framing, not as exerting influence in isolation
constraints: The unity of demands cannot be predicted in advance but emerges in the dynamic interplay of humans, technologies, institutional structures, and norms
target_learners: higher education students working with GenAI
target_learning_goals: participating in academic practices with GenAI in ways valued within those practices
examples: Domain-internal demand example: that GenAI can be biased due to bias in the training data; activity-framing example: not handing in a report as one's own that was written by someone else
key_sources: Sun, Z., Dohn, N. B., & Rehm, M. (2026). Literacy Demands Placed on Students in Student–GenAI Entanglements in Higher Education. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00697-7

article_title: Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Taylor Martin & Bruce Sherin. (2013). Learning Analytics and Computational Techniques for Detecting and Evaluating Patterns in Learning: An Introduction to the Special Issue. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 22(4), 511–520. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.840466
title: Do not let ease of data collection or fit with analytics tools restrict what learning phenomena are studied or what questions are asked
description: The article closes with cautions for learning scientists adopting LA. It warns: "we must not restrict ourselves to collecting only the data that are easy to collect," because mouse clicks and key presses "provide only a limited picture of a learning activity" even at the computer, and many learning activities involve no computer at all. It further warns against letting LA shape the research agenda: "it is essential that we do not compromise, that we use LA where it helps us to answer our core questions rather than as the sole guide of what questions to ask."
requirements: Researchers must continue studying learning across contexts—at home and in school, indoors and outdoors—and keep theory primary when framing research questions.
constraints: The principle is stated as a caution for the learning sciences community adopting LA; the article notes LA can also be applied to traditional data such as interview transcripts, as in Sherin's article.
target_learners: Learning sciences researchers and educational designers adopting learning analytics
target_learning_goals: Preserving theoretical integrity and ecological breadth in learning research that uses analytics
examples: The article points to Sherin's contribution as evidence that LA can be applied to traditional interview transcript data rather than only clickstream logs.

article_title: The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic
citation: Camilla Gilmore, Sarah Keeble, Sophie Richardson, Lucy Cragg. (2015). The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic. ZDM Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-014-0659-y
title: Dot comparison congruency-effect measure of numerical inhibition
description: A novel technique for assessing inhibition in a numerical context without Arabic digits: participants compare two dot arrays and select the more numerous set while ignoring dot size and array area. The article states that "incongruent trials, but not congruent trials carry a heavy inhibition load", so the difference in performance between congruent and incongruent trials provides a measure of inhibition skill. The authors showed this measure relates to a standard inhibition task and to mathematics achievement, predicting performance even after accounting for non-numerical inhibition.
requirements: Participants must ignore the visual characteristics (dot size, density, area) of the arrays and respond based on number of dots only
constraints: The measure indexes interference control, not response inhibition; the article notes further research with a variety of inhibition tasks is required
target_learners: 11- to 12-year-olds
13- to 14-year-olds
young adults
target_learning_goals: arithmetic achievement
inhibitory control in numerical contexts
examples: In the study, participants completed 6 practice trials and 80 experimental dot comparison trials, with dot numbers ranging from 5 to 28 and ratios from 0.5 to 0.8
key_sources: Camilla Gilmore, Sarah Keeble, Sophie Richardson, Lucy Cragg. (2015). The role of cognitive inhibition in different components of arithmetic. ZDM Mathematics Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11858-014-0659-y

article_title: Developmental Changes in the Profiles of Dyscalculia: An Explanation Based on a Double Exact-and-Approximate Number Representation Model
citation: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165
title: Double exact-and-approximate number representation model: an exact representation of numerical value built from symbolic number learning, alongside the approximate number system
description: The article proposes that human number cognition rests on two semantic representations: the approximate number system (ANS), shared with animals and yielding noisy magnitude estimates, and an exact representation of numerical value that emerges only through learning symbolic numbers embedded in a counting sequence. The authors argue that "the learning of symbolic numbers would lead to the emergence of a new numerical representation system in human ontogeny," endowed with semantic content based on the ordinal information in the symbol sequence. They use this model to explain the developmental profile of DD: the first deficit concerns building the exact representation, while reduced ANS acuity is a later, secondary consequence.
requirements: Learning of a number system based on the successor function and embedded in a counting process
constraints: The exact representation of large numbers develops only given a counting system; cultures with very limited number lexicon do not develop it beyond 3 or 4, per the evidence the article cites
target_learners: children in typical and atypical numerical development
children with developmental dyscalculia
target_learning_goals: understanding the cardinal meaning of symbolic numbers
building exact representations of natural numbers
examples: The article contrasts this model with the 'simple story' in which number words take their meaning by mapping directly onto the ANS
key_sources: Noël M-P and Rousselle L (2011) Developmental changes in the profiles of dyscalculia: an explanation based on a double exact-and-approximate number representation model. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 5:165. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2011.00165

article_title: Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation
citation: Teresa Sosa, Allison H. Hall, and Susan R. Goldman; Carol D. Lee. (2015). Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation.
title: Domain analysis of literary interpretation: levels of text representation plus point-driven reading
description: The article's domain analysis identifies components of competent literary analysis, grounding basic comprehension in a cognitive discourse processing approach in which "comprehension results in different “levels” of representation of a text, most commonly described as surface code, textbase, and situation model." Because literary reading is "point-driven," the authors postulate additional levels of representation beyond the situation model, so readers construct mental models of the author's possible intentions. The analysis also specifies that valid interpretations rest on textual evidence plus reasoning connecting evidence to interpretive claims, drawing on worldviews and knowledge of other texts.
requirements: Instruction must address multiple foci: textbase and situation model building, rhetorical strategies, and evidence-plus-reasoning for interpretive claims
constraints: The authors note few instructional efforts integrated multiple foci, with Lee's Cultural Modeling Framework as the exception they cite
target_learners: adolescent secondary students in English Language Arts
target_learning_goals: literary analysis and interpretation
making and warranting interpretive claims about symbolism
examples: The module design derived learning objectives from this analysis, sequencing symbol identification, text-evidence-based claims, and patterns of evidence across extended texts.
key_sources: Teresa Sosa, Allison H. Hall, and Susan R. Goldman; Carol D. Lee. (2015). Developing Symbolic Interpretation Through Literary Argumentation. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2015.1124040

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Domain-structuredness hypothesis: PF effectiveness may be restricted to structured domains
description: The article argues that PF requires a canonical solution whose components can be compared and contrasted with features of erroneous student ideas during instruction. It reports that "Loibl et al. (2017) hypothesize that the effectiveness of PF may only emerge for learning in structured domains, which \"allow for clear identification of deep features and evaluation of solution attempts\" (p. 712)". It situates social science research-methods topics on a continuum as "rather structured topics", less structured than STEM topics like standard deviation but still evaluable, making them an apt test case for transferring PF beyond STEM.
requirements: The targeted concept should have a canonical or established solution whose crucial components can be presented and explained during instruction
The problem should remain complex and allow students to generate different solution ideas
constraints: Discipline traditions can vary the principles and criteria deemed appropriate, so non-STEM topics are typically less structured than STEM topics
target_learners: secondary school students
target_learning_goals: learning research methods and scientific practices in the social sciences
examples: The article contrasts the standard deviation topic of Kapur's studies with social/educational science topics like social inequality (little structure) and experimental design analysis (rather structured).
key_sources: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2

article_title: Complete or faded double-content examples of video-based analyses: How do they impact student teachers’ professional vision of classroom management?
citation: Jasmin Lilian Bauersfeld, Bernadette Gold. (2025). Complete or faded double-content examples of video-based analyses: How do they impact student teachers' professional vision of classroom management? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09738-3
title: Double-content examples as instructional support for video-based analysis in an ill-structured domain
description: Double-content examples integrate two levels: the learning domain level (the skill being taught, here analyzing classroom videos) and the exemplifying domain level (the content illustrating it, here classroom management). In this study, written analyses by an expert teacher with 38 years of experience served as examples, with highlighted text sequences marking professional vision indicators and instructional explanations added. The framework draws on cognitive load theory and the worked example effect, proposing that novices study expert solutions before producing their own analyses.
requirements: Learners study the double-content examples before conducting their own video-based analyses
constraints: The study found the examples hindered some professional vision outcomes in this ill-structured domain, so the framework's benefit in teacher education is not supported by this study
target_learners: student teachers (pre-service elementary teachers)
target_learning_goals: professional vision of classroom management: noticing, reasoning, generating alternatives of action, and expert features
examples: Three text-based double-content examples were developed from an expert teacher's written video-based analyses, with indicators highlighted in yellow, blue, and green, and validated with five experienced teachers in think-aloud interviews
key_sources: Jasmin Lilian Bauersfeld, Bernadette Gold. (2025). Complete or faded double-content examples of video-based analyses: How do they impact student teachers' professional vision of classroom management? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09738-3

article_title: Teaching sourcing during online inquiry – adolescents with the weakest skills benefited the most
citation: Hämäläinen, E. K., Kiili, C., Räikkönen, E., Lakkala, M., Ilomäki, L., Toom, A., & Marttunen, M. (2023). Teaching sourcing during online inquiry – adolescents with the weakest skills benefited the most. Instructional Science, 51, 135–163. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09597-2
title: Documents Model and Online Research and Comprehension Model as the framework for sourcing throughout online inquiry
description: The study is informed by two theoretical models. The Online Research and Comprehension Model frames online inquiry as five recursive, reciprocal processes: "specifying information need and locating, critically evaluating, synthesizing, and communicating online information". The Documents Model holds that "readers can construct two types of representations when reading multiple texts: an intertext model and an integrated mental model", with source-to-content and source-to-source links connecting source information to content and across documents. The intervention and its scoring rubrics were designed around these models, treating sourcing as applicable in every inquiry phase.
requirements: Sourcing instruction should be structured to follow the phases of online inquiry so that source information is attended to in each phase
constraints: The Documents Model was initially developed in the context of interpreting historical documents, and the article applies it to online health information
target_learners: upper secondary school students
target_learning_goals: sourcing during online inquiry
critical evaluation of online information
multiple document comprehension

article_title: Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour
citation: Anders Bouwer, Bert Bredeweg. (2010). Graphical means for inspecting qualitative models of system behaviour. Instr Sci 38:173–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9083-4
title: Guiding principles for a domain-independent diagrammatic vocabulary for model inspection
description: To design VISIGARP's visualizations the authors laid down guiding principles, e.g. "Information related to a speciﬁc entity is displayed within the visual element representing that entity, using the container-metaphor as much as possible" and displaying relationships as separate connecting elements, showing context-dependent information within its context, using labelled links to distinguish multiple relationship types, and offering display toggles when multiple information types are combined. The approach deliberately avoids domain-specific symbols to remain usable across domains and drawable by hand.
requirements: Visual primitives (shapes, arrows, indentation, meaningful space) combined into views supporting specific reasoning tasks
constraints: The article notes the no-rotation rule for text can place arrows against the normal reading direction, causing readability problems such as in diagrams test question 6
target_learners: novice learners inspecting qualitative simulations
target_learning_goals: interpreting model structure, states, and causal dependencies from diagrams
examples: States are shown as numbered circles, entities as labelled boxes, quantities as round-edged boxes with vertically ordered quantity spaces, and derivatives as small black triangles or circles

article_title: Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes
citation: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x
title: Do not implement perceptual disfluency (degraded fonts) as an instructional intervention
description: The editorial draws a direct instructional recommendation from the special issue's null results: perceptual disfluency via degraded fonts should not be implemented in educational settings, because all 13 experiments failed to show better performance and the effect appears marginal or condition-bound. The authors state: "results further question the positive impact of disfluency interventions in educational settings, and we would not recommend implementing them." This recommendation is grounded in the special issue's systematic tests of moderators and mediators.
requirements: Sound experimentation and sufficient sample size, as required for inclusion in the special issue, to establish that null effects are meaningful boundary conditions rather than methodological flaws
constraints: The recommendation concerns perceptual disfluency manipulations (fonts, blurring, greyscale); the authors note it does not necessarily generalize to stronger difficulties such as deleting words from a passage
target_learners: university students
school pupils
target_learning_goals: retention and comprehension of instructional materials
reasoning task performance
examples: The special issue assembled six manuscripts with 13 experiments and more than 1000 participants testing disfluency effects on recall, comprehension, transfer, and metacognitive monitoring
key_sources: Tim Kühl & Alexander Eitel. (2016). Effects of disfluency on cognitive and metacognitive processes and outcomes. Metacognition and Learning, 11, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-016-9154-x

article_title: The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review
citation: Anmarkrud, Ø., Bråten, I., Florit, E., & Mason, L. (2022). The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09640-7
title: Documents model framework: source-content and source-source links constitute the intertext model
description: The documents model framework (Perfetti et al., 1999), built on Kintsch's construction-integration model, holds that readers of multiple documents represent both an integrated situations model of content and source information. The review explains that "the source-content links and the source-source links described above constitute the intertext model within the documents model framework", which is required to judge content in light of its source and understand relationships between sources. The framework grounds the review's expectation that disciplinary expertise influences intertext model construction.
requirements: A complete documents model requires the situations model to be supplemented and integrated with an intertext model
constraints: The framework was originally focused on reconciling accounts of historical events, later extended to other domains
target_learners: readers of multiple documents across educational levels
target_learning_goals: multiple document literacy
sourcing
critical reading
examples: The review traces the framework's origin to Wineburg's (1991) observation that expert historians attended to author, document type, and date before judging evidentiary value

article_title: Correlates of K-12 Students’ Intertextual Integration
citation: Daniel R. Espinas, Brennan W. Chandler. (2024). Correlates of K-12 Students' Intertextual Integration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09889-8
title: Documents Model Framework: integration via an integrated situations model and an inter-text model
description: The Documents Model Framework (DMF; Britt et al., 1999; Perfetti et al., 1999) is the review's anchor theoretical account of how meaning is constructed from multiple documents. It proposes that "integration is accomplished by constructing two representations: an integrated situations model and an inter-text model" — the situations model holds semantic content about the common topic, while the inter-text model holds meta-document information such as source author, publication, date, and purpose. The review describes three possible representational outcomes: a mush model, a separate representations model, and a documents model, and notes the DMF "provided the foundation for much of the theorizing and empirical work that has followed."
requirements: Tasks and contexts in which well-formed intertextual representations matter, such as history-class research reports, for readers to construct a documents model
constraints: The likelihood a reader constructs a particular representational form depends in part on the context and task at hand; effortful connection formation may not occur when readers view connections as unnecessary or are unable to form them
target_learners: K-12 students reading multiple text documents
target_learning_goals: Constructing coherent integrated representations of situations presented across multiple documents, including linking content to sources
examples: The review uses the DMF to organize its taxonomy of individual difference predictors and illustrates the three representational outcomes (mush model, separate representations model, documents model) in Fig. 1
key_sources: Daniel R. Espinas, Brennan W. Chandler. (2024). Correlates of K-12 Students' Intertextual Integration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09889-8

article_title: Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years’ Research
citation: Sébastien Miravete, André Tricot. (2024). Are Some People Generally More Creative Than Others? A Systematic Review of Fifty Years' Research. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09926-6
title: Three variants of the domain-general creativity hypothesis: mechanist, minimalist, and maximalist
description: The review organizes claims that creativity is domain-general into three non-equivalent variants. The mechanist variant holds that "the cognitive or neural mechanisms involved in creative tasks are domain-general". The minimalist variant requires general factors with a non-negligible positive impact (e.g., Cohen's d ≥ 0.2) that are all teachable; the maximalist variant requires at least one unteachable general factor, such as a genetic one. The variants carry different educational consequences: minimalism supports teaching general creativity, maximalism supports selecting potentially creative individuals.
requirements: A theory of creativity must specify which general factors it posits and whether they are teachable, since the three variants imply different educational recommendations
constraints: Minimalism and maximalism are not compatible with each other, though the mechanistic hypothesis is compatible with both
target_learners: students
employees in vocational training
target_learning_goals: creative performance across domains
examples: The review classifies its 36 selected studies by these variants in Table 1's last column

article_title: Peer Spillover and Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effects with SIMS80: Revisiting a Historical Database Through the Lens of a Modern Methodological Perspective
citation: Televantou, I., Marsh, H. W., Xu, K. M., Guo, J., & Dicke, T. (2023). Peer Spillover and Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effects with SIMS80: Revisiting a Historical Database Through the Lens of a Modern Methodological Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09816-3
title: Doubly latent models for compositional effects
description: Doubly latent models are multilevel latent variable models that estimate compositional effects while correcting for two sources of error: measurement error in individual-level measures, controlled "by using multiple indicators," and sampling error in aggregates, "adjusted for by using latent rather than a manifest aggregation to form the group-level aggregates." The article applies multi-group doubly latent models in Mplus 8 to SIMS80 data to test peer spillover and BFLPE effects, showing they change substantive conclusions relative to manifest models.
requirements: Multiple indicators of the individual-level construct to control measurement error
Latent aggregation of group-level measures to adjust sampling error
Longitudinal or otherwise controlled data supporting prior-achievement controls
constraints: The article notes concern about overcorrecting for sampling error with intact classes, though juxtaposed latent-manifest estimates showed no substantial differences
target_learners: secondary school students (13-year-old mathematics students)
target_learning_goals: estimating class-level compositional effects on achievement and academic self-concept
examples: Multi-group doubly latent models applied to SIMS80 pre- and post-test mathematics achievement and four-item mathematics self-concept measures

article_title: Dosage Response in Intensive Mathematics Interventions for Early Elementary Students With or At-Risk for Mathematics Learning Disability
citation: Anna H. Miller, Daniel R. Espinas, Daniel McNeish, & Marcia A. Barnes. (2025). Dosage Response in Intensive Mathematics Interventions for Early Elementary Students With or At-Risk for Mathematics Learning Disability. Educational Psychology Review, 37, 91. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10070-y
title: Dose–response framework with dosage defined as cumulative intensity (session duration × frequency × treatment length)
description: The article applies the dose–response framework, borrowed from medicine and pharmacology, to academic intervention: the dose–response curve represents the relation between an intervention's intensity and its effects. Dosage is operationalized following Warren et al. (2007) as "the product of an intervention's session duration (e.g., 30 min), frequency (e.g., three times per week), and length of treatment (e.g., 15 weeks)", quantified as total instructional hours per student. The framework distinguishes a linear dose–response relation, where "the effect of the treatment increases in direct proportion to the amount of treatment delivered", from a nonlinear one that peaks and then plateaus or diminishes. The authors use it to test whether K-3 mathematics interventions show diminishing returns as reading interventions do.
requirements: Studies must adequately report intervention frequency, duration, and length so dosage can be calculated as total hours per student
constraints: Analyses excluded computerized or partially computerized interventions and adaptive/SMART designs, so the framework's application here is limited to human-delivered, fixed-dosage interventions compared to non-active controls
target_learners: Kindergarten through third grade students with or at risk for mathematics learning disability
target_learning_goals: Foundational mathematics skills including number knowledge, operations, and word-problem solving
examples: The authors meta-analyzed 164 effect sizes from 24 studies with dosages ranging from 3.12 to 42.0 hours (Mdn = 20 h) using this framework
key_sources: Anna H. Miller, Daniel R. Espinas, Daniel McNeish, & Marcia A. Barnes. (2025). Dosage Response in Intensive Mathematics Interventions for Early Elementary Students With or At-Risk for Mathematics Learning Disability. article_title: Teacher self-efficacy, instructional quality, and student motivational beliefs: An analysis using multilevel structural equation modeling
citation: Burić, Irena and Kim, Lisa (2020) Teacher self-efficacy, instructional quality, and student motivational beliefs: An analysis using multilevel structural equation modeling. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101302
title: Doubly latent multilevel structural equation modeling for climate-effect research
description: The article employs doubly latent multilevel SEM (Marsh et al., 2009) to test relationships between teacher and classroom constructs at the correct level of analysis. Its stated advantages are "the ability to control for measurement error at both L1 and L2 levels by using multiple indicators of a construct, as well as the ability to control for sampling error through the aggregating individual student responses to represent teacher level characteristic". It treats instructional quality as a classroom climate effect with the class, not the individual student, as referent.
requirements: Students nested within teachers, with each student rating the same teacher-referent classroom characteristic so aggregation at the teacher level is valid.
constraints: The article notes many classroom constructs must be tested at the teacher level; residual student-level ratings may reflect method effects rather than substantive climate.
target_learners: high school students in grammar-school programs
target_learning_goals: student self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation in subject-specific learning
examples: The study aggregated reports from on average 22 students per teacher to form latent teacher-level constructs while controlling measurement and sampling error.
key_sources: Burić, Irena and Kim, Lisa (2020) Teacher self-efficacy, instructional quality, and student motivational beliefs: An analysis using multilevel structural equation modeling. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2019.101302

article_title: Reading comprehension resiliency in adolescents with and without dyslexia relates to vocabulary, listening comprehension and socioeconomic status
citation: Lefèvre, E., Law, J. M., Prado, J., Anders, R., & Cavalli, E. (2024). Reading Comprehension Resiliency in Adolescents with and without Dyslexia relates to Vocabulary, Listening Comprehension and Socioeconomic Status. https://osf.io/fzyeh/?view_only=84fc51248a0d48ba9a505835e525efdc
title: Double mediation model of reading comprehension resiliency linking SES, vocabulary, listening comprehension and RCR
description: The article proposes and tests a double mediation model in which "the relationship between SES and listening comprehension is mediated by vocabulary", and "the direct effect of vocabulary on RCR is mediated by listening comprehension". RCR is operationalized as a continuous index computed by subtracting standardized reading fluency from standardized reading comprehension, so positive values reflect high comprehension despite low fluency. The fitted model retained direct paths and showed excellent fit on standard SEM diagnostics.
requirements: Assessment of vocabulary, listening comprehension, reading fluency and reading comprehension on comparable standardized scales
A sample large enough for the number of estimated path parameters (the article cites a 10-observations-per-parameter minimum)
constraints: The design is correlational and cross-sectional, so the model supports no causal claims; alternative models could also fit the findings
The sample over-represents individuals with dyslexia relative to the general population, limiting generalisability
target_learners: Adolescents with dyslexia
Adolescents without reading impairments
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension development
Vocabulary and listening comprehension as semantic supports for reading
examples: A path analysis on 95 French adolescents fit the double mediation model with excellent SEM diagnostics (X² = 0.02, p = .89; CFI = 1.00), and bootstrapped standard errors (n = 3000) replicated the initial results

article_title: Which class matters? Juxtaposing multiple class environments as frames-of-reference for academic self-concept formation.
citation: Fleischmann, M., Hübner, N., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Trautwein, U., & Nagengast, B. (2021). Which Class Matters? Juxtaposing Multiple Class Environments as Frames-of-Reference for Academic Self-Concept Formation.
title: When placing students in high-achieving classes, weigh domain-specific classes most heavily for self-concept costs
description: In course-by-course tracked systems, grouping decisions should anticipate that the BFLPE is strongest in the domain-specific class: students' self-concept "may be hurt when placing them in high achieving domain-specific classes" and "to a lesser extent also be hurt when placing them in high achieving domain-unrelated classrooms." Placement policy should therefore prioritize the achievement composition of domain-specific classes when managing self-concept risks.
requirements: A course-by-course tracked system in which students belong to both domain-specific and domain-unrelated class environments
constraints: Findings are limited to mathematics self-concept among Austrian eighth-graders in 2012
target_learners: eighth-grade students in course-by-course tracked systems
target_learning_goals: protecting academic self-concept under ability grouping
examples: The study refined BFLPE implications for course-by-course tracked systems using population-wide Austrian data with cross-classified multilevel models.

article_title: Do Spanish-English bilingual children outperform monolingual English-speaking children on executive function tasks in early childhood? A propensity score analysis.
citation: Goodrich, J. M., Koziol, N. A., Yoon, H., & Leiva, S. (2019). Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Doebel's ecological framework: executive function develops in the context of goal-directed behavior
description: The article adopts Doebel's (2020) re-conceptualization of executive function, which criticizes componential models (e.g., the tripartite and unity/diversity models) for isolating EF components from the contexts in which they develop. Instead, "a more appropriate theoretical framework would involve conceptualizing and measuring EF as skills that develop in the context of a need to achieve specific goals." Under this view, children's experiences, knowledge, values, and cultural norms shape goals, and environment interactions in service of goals drive EF development. The study uses this framework to predict bilingual advantages on ecologically valid, report-based measures rather than abstract laboratory tasks.
requirements: Measures of EF should capture the real-world contexts in which children use EF in pursuit of goals, such as teacher or parent report questionnaires
constraints: The article notes it was unable to account for cultural heterogeneity among different populations of Spanish speakers within its sample
target_learners: early childhood (kindergarten) children
target_learning_goals: executive function development, including inhibitory control, attentional focus, working memory, and cognitive flexibility
examples: The study tested the framework by comparing report-based (CBQ) and performance-based (DCCS, Numbers Reversed) EF measures in a matched bilingual-monolingual comparison

article_title: The effect of prediction error on episodic memory encoding is modulated by the outcome of the predictions
citation: Francesco Pupillo, Javier Ortiz-Tudela, Rasmus Bruckner and Yee Lee Shing. (2023). The effect of prediction error on episodic memory encoding is modulated by the outcome of the predictions. npj Science of Learning 8:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00166-x
title: Hippocampal-striatal dopaminergic account of outcome-modulated prediction-error effects on encoding
description: The article proposes that interactions between the striatal and hippocampal dopaminergic systems explain why prediction error helps memory after correct predictions and harms it after incorrect ones. When "the expectation of a certain outcome was low, a correct prediction might nevertheless provide a PE signal which increases the release of dopamine in the striatum, promoting hippocampal activation, and resulting in better encoding". Conversely, when an outcome is strongly expected, an incorrect prediction corresponds to a negative PE that suppresses striatal dopamine release and hippocampal activation, resulting in impaired encoding. The article draws on evidence that dopamine enhances long-term potentiation in the hippocampus and that increased striatum-hippocampus connectivity may lead to enhanced memory encoding.
requirements: Future studies investigating the connectivity between the hippocampus and striatum at these different conditions are needed to provide support for these hypotheses, per the article
constraints: The recognition task used does not allow the authors to conclude whether recognition performance is driven by recollection or by familiarity processes, so hippocampal involvement is not established
target_learners: young adults learning probabilistic context-object associations
target_learning_goals: episodic encoding of novel items under established prior expectations
examples: The article interprets its two-experiment contingency-learning paradigm, in which prediction outcome moderated PE effects on recognition, through this dopaminergic mechanism
key_sources: Francesco Pupillo, Javier Ortiz-Tudela, Rasmus Bruckner and Yee Lee Shing. (2023). The effect of prediction error on episodic memory encoding is modulated by the outcome of the predictions. npj Science of Learning 8:18. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00166-x

article_title: Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning
citation: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4
title: Embed relational reasoning training within academic domains rather than teaching it generically
description: The article recommends that efforts to foster relational reasoning not be treated as generic skills. As the author states, "relational reasoning training should not be isolated from the content with which students are typically or routinely engaged", and should instead be naturally nested within the academic domains framing students' educational experience. This rests on the strategy-training literature's finding that entirely generic efforts are less likely to have lasting effects, and on the article's argument that educators must recognize analogies, anomalies, antitheses, and antinomies in the subjects they teach.
requirements: Educators must themselves be familiar and comfortable with all forms of relational reasoning and their manifestations in schooling content
constraints: The precise form of explicit training, especially its domain specificity, remains an open question in the article
target_learners: students across K-12 and higher education in domains such as reading, history, mathematics, science, and medicine
target_learning_goals: analogical, anomalous, antithetical, and antinomous reasoning within domain content
examples: The article cites Murphy et al.'s elaborated-explanation writing training and Greene et al.'s exploratory-talk training as domain-embedded approaches that increased analogical, antithetical, and anomalous reasoning in student products and discussion
key_sources: Patricia A Alexander. (2016). Relational thinking and relational reasoning: harnessing the power of patterning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/npjscilearn.2016.4

article_title: Questioning central assumptions of the ICAP framework
citation: Thurn, C. M., Edelsbrunner, P. A., Berkowitz, M., Deiglmayr, A. & Schalk, L. (2023). Questioning central assumptions of the ICAP framework. npj Science of Learning 8:49. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00197-4
title: Do not rely on the ICAP framework alone for selecting interventions or assessing learning in the classroom
description: Because overt behaviors are ambiguous with respect to underlying learning processes and the I > C > A > P hierarchy lacks a convincing empirical basis, the comment concludes that "practitioners should not be advised to rely on ICAP for selecting effective interventions and assessing learning processes in the classroom". Instead, changes in knowledge components can only be detected via deliberate assessment. Judging engagement from two susceptible sources — overt behaviors and student output — risks wrong inferences in practice.
requirements: Practitioners need evidence-based tools that are practical in everyday teaching; deliberate assessment events are necessary to gain insight into students' learning processes.
constraints: The ICAP framework itself provides no guidance on how to generate and use diagnostic information on students' covert learning processes.
target_learners: Teachers and instructional designers
target_learning_goals: Selecting effective interventions and accurately assessing students' learning processes
examples: The comment argues that relying primarily on overt behavior to plan, monitor, and judge instructional events bears the risk of distorting insights into actual covert learning processes.

article_title: Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing
citation: Mengzhou Li, Lei Luo, Sujoy Sikdar, Navid Ibtehaj Nizam, Shan Gao, Hongming Shan, Melanie Kruger, Uwe Kruger, Hisham Mohamed, Lirong Xia and Ge Wang. (2021). Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3
title: DOT platform: a web application delivering individualized, synchronized question sequences for distanced online testing, with publicly released source code
description: The DOT platform is a web application the authors developed and applied to a real undergraduate final exam. It "incorporat[es] the anti-collusion techniques as well as other complementary techniques for online exams", presenting each student their own set of M1 questions one by one in predetermined time slots without revisiting previous questions, with a WebEx session available during the exam for instructor support. The source codes and simulation data are publicly available on Github (https://github.com/edward1001001/Anticheating_in_DOT).
requirements: A question pool of M2 questions and estimates of student competences to construct the colluding matrix and optimize assignments
constraints: Mainly designed for math or fact-based courses; illustrated with multiple-choice questions, though compatible with most question types except easy-writing-type tests
target_learners: undergraduate students taking remote online exams
target_learning_goals: valid remote assessment of learning outcomes
examples: Used for the final exam of an undergraduate imaging course on 28 April 2020 with 78 of 85 students participating.

Optimized collusion prevention for online exams during social distancing. npj Science of Learning 6:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00083-3

article_title: Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning
citation: Zhu, J.-P., Xie, X.-Y., Yu, C. & Zhang, J.-Y. (2026). Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00396-1
title: To promote transfer of location-specific learning, expose the transfer context concurrently with or after primary training, not before
description: The article's double-training principle holds that pairing primary training with passive or interleaved exposure to the transfer context enables generalization, but only when that exposure is "concurrently with or after II learning", not before it. In the experiments, an irrelevant contrast discrimination task at the mirror-symmetric location reduced location specificity when interleaved with or following the II category task, but abolished transfer when it preceded category training. The authors extend this to practice design: "varying stimulus presentation and incorporating spaced, multi-context practice can strengthen abstract memory traces, reduce context dependence, and foster flexible knowledge transfer".
requirements: A primary task trained at one location plus an irrelevant task providing exposure at the transfer location, with the transfer-location exposure occurring during or after primary learning
constraints: Transfer was markedly weaker when exposure to the transfer location preceded category learning; all experiments ran within a single 1-1.5-hour session, so the authors caution the similarity to perceptual learning principles should be interpreted cautiously
target_learners: Adult learners in perceptual and category-learning training, including clinical rehabilitation populations
target_learning_goals: Generalization of trained categorization or discrimination skill to untrained locations and contexts
examples: Experiment 2 interleaved eight blocks of contrast discrimination at the transfer location with the II category task; Experiment 4 placed the II task first and the contrast task second; both showed comparable post-test accuracy across locations, whereas Experiment 3's reversed order left a large deficit

article_title: Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion
citation: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8
title: Distinction between domain-relevant task-proximal and domain-irrelevant task-distal uncertainty
description: The article proposes that uncertainty is not monolithic and can be categorized by domain relevance and task proximity. Domain-relevant, task-proximal uncertainties "directly implicate students' goals", while domain-irrelevant, task-distal uncertainties, "while strong, may not readily translate into curious behaviors within the educational sphere". This account explains why seasonal exam uncertainty consistently elevated question-posing across topics while COVID-19 uncertainty did not. The authors argue future researchers should differentiate among forms of uncertainty rather than assuming uniform links with curious behaviors.
requirements: Future studies differentiating forms of uncertainty by domain relevance and task proximity
constraints: The two dimensions were not independently isolated in this study — educational periods and the COVID-19 pandemic differed on both simultaneously, so their independent contributions cannot be definitively identified
target_learners: adolescent students in online learning communities
target_learning_goals: understanding how situational uncertainty shapes curious behaviors
examples: Exam periods represent structured, predictable, academically consequential uncertainty; the COVID-19 pandemic represented unstructured, unpredictable global disruption without clear links to students' immediate needs.
key_sources: Ali, F., Yang, Y., & Poh, J.-H. (2026). Curious behaviors in times of uncertainty: dynamics of student question-posing in online educational discussion. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00440-8

article_title: Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes
citation: Mejia-Domenzain, P., Frej, J., Neshaei, S. P., Mouchel, L., Nazaretsky, T., Wambsganss, T., Bosselut, A., & Käser, T. (2025). Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1
title: Double-content examples in heuristic domains: examples must be processed on a learning-domain and an exemplifying-domain level
description: The article frames example-based learning in heuristic domains (where no algorithmic solution exists, such as cooking recipes) through the notion of double-content examples. Learners must process two content levels: "(1) the learning domain (i.e., how to structure the solution) and (2) the exemplifying domain (i.e., the topic)". In structural domains examples are annotated with solution steps, whereas double-content examples are enriched with self-explanation prompts and instructional explanations. RELEX instantiates this framing in procedural writing.
requirements: Examples in heuristic domains must be enriched, e.g., with self-explanation prompts or instructional explanations, because learners process two content levels
constraints: Applies to heuristic domains with no single correct solution; prior work noted static examples and explanations can be redundant or not timely
target_learners: Learners composing procedural texts in heuristic domains, e.g., culinary students
target_learning_goals: Acquiring heuristics for structuring and writing high-quality procedural texts
examples: A cooking-recipe learner must understand procedural text structure (learning domain) while being familiar with cooking (exemplifying domain)

Enhancing Procedural Writing Through Personalized Example Retrieval: A Case Study on Cooking Recipes. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00405-1

article_title: Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors
citation: Antonija Mitrovic & Pramuditha Suraweera. (2016). Teaching Database Design with Constraint-Based Tutors. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:448–456. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0084-6
title: Distinction between instructional domains and instructional tasks in analyzing ill-definedness
description: The article applies Mitrovic and Weerasinghe's (2009) distinction between instructional domains and instructional tasks when discussing ill-definedness. The ER model itself is well-defined, with a handful of constructs with well-defined syntax, but conceptual database design using the ER model is an ill-defined task: requirements are underspecified and ambiguous, there is no algorithm to produce ER schemas, the stopping criterion is unclear, and there is no best solution but "rather a family of solutions for each problem". These features are typical of design tasks in general.
requirements: Understanding the application domain, common sense and background knowledge to interpret requirements
constraints: Checking semantic correctness requires ensuring the schema covers requirements completely and is of high quality, which is much harder than checking syntactic correctness
target_learners: students learning design tasks such as database modeling
target_learning_goals: conceptual database design; understanding ill-defined problem solving
examples: The article contrasts ER modeling with SQL query writing, where solutions are more structured because queries consist of six clauses

article_title: Everyone already has their community beyond the screen: reconceptualizing online learning and expanding boundaries
citation: Kyungmee Lee. (2018). Everyone already has their community beyond the screen: reconceptualizing online learning and expanding boundaries. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-9613-y
title: Double-layered CoP model of online learning
description: The double-layered CoP model conceptualizes online learning as "interlinked processes of participation and socialization in multiple communities across online- and ofﬂine-''layers'' of learners' lives". It was originally developed by incorporating CoP principles into an online teacher education course addressing divisions between teachers' online learning and their classroom teaching. The model guides online course designers to expand the perceived boundaries of the course environments they design to include learners' offline learning contexts, rather than focusing exclusively on building a single community within an online course.
requirements: The course must explicitly guide students to choose and develop one of their existing communities into a supportive CoP, as a student-driven process
constraints: The author states the suggested principles are more relevant and applicable to online course design than face-to-face course design
target_learners: adult online learners in higher education, particularly in-service teachers and working professionals
target_learning_goals: authentically constructivist learning through participation and socialization in communities of practice
examples: Jane's 12-week online course required structured CoP journal entries reflecting on developing external CoPs and connecting course ideas to practices in them

article_title: Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina
citation: Banegas, D.L., & Manzur Busleimán, G. (2014). Motivating factors in online language teacher education in southern Argentina. Computers & Education, 76, 131–142. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2014.03.014
title: Do not make forum participation or group-work tasks mandatory in online teacher education
description: The authors argue that because trainees may not value collaborative learning, "forum participation or group-work tasks should not be mandatory." They recommend trainees be allowed to choose collaborative processes and instances, for example by starting their own forum threads and posing their own questions. title: doktormitSDM didactic framework: in-situ ultrashort feedback, handling of control, and stimulated continuous self-observation
description: The training rests on a didactic concept addressing feasibility, clinician barriers, and sustainable transfer. Feasibility is pursued by delivering the interactive component at the participant's ward: the authors "presumed that behaviour change was most likely to happen when the interactive part of the training was provided at the participant's ward (in situ) and shaped and structured as an ultrashort unit of 15 minutes." Behaviour change is addressed via attitude-related beliefs, subjective social norms and behaviour control, with feedback kept explicitly qualitative and non-judgemental to avoid devaluation. Control is handled as the key to learning potential: voluntary relinquishment of control through delivering one's own work samples, and re-transferal of control through transparency, is meant to model a good doctor–patient dialogue and induce self-observation even in the trainer's absence.
requirements: Feedback must be recognizable as both highly professional and precise in its detailed descriptions and explicitly qualitative
Trainers must adapt to each trainee's SDM level and continuously evaluate the trainees' capacity and tolerance
constraints: Marginal discrepancies between training content or context and the doctors' reality might give reason to adopt a rejecting stance
Feedback must be stopped before resistance rises

medical students (adapted online version being tested)
target_learning_goals: shared decision-making communication

examples: The trainer asks questions to stimulate the trainee's self-observation instead of valuing actions as good or bad
